extracted.intended_audience: public relations practitioners and managers (PR departments, communicators producing slide/film/media presentations)
extracted.subtask_description: Planning, scripting, producing, and evaluating slide shows, multimedia presentations, and PR films — including equipment selection, budgeting, pretesting, and visual design — for public-relations audiences. Emphasizes matching message and form, practical production steps, and common faults to avoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and clarity of message
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex visual presentations may arouse interest and emotions but not communicate a message; 'If you want a clear message to come across, don’t make your presentation too complex.' Slide shows rarely change attitudes and behaviors, though they have a slightly better chance than still photographs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer simplicity: avoid unnecessary visual complexity that obscures the intended points. Use only as much visual complexity as needed to support the objectives; favor clarity over spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pretesting and audience evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: It is too intrusive to hand out questionnaires to members of an audience that has just seen a slide show; instead, pretest the slide show on a sample audience and use questionnaires similar to those described in Chapter 9.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use trial audiences, questionnaires, or signaled stopping techniques to measure objectives. For films, use an Audience Analyzer (or script copies and stop-recording as a substitute) to record interest, boredom, agreement, confusion and correlate responses with sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of signaled-stopping (trial audience) technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide people with a list of slides and ask them to indicate next to a slide description whenever they feel like stopping—for reasons such as confusion, agreement, or understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use signaled stopping to identify confusing or unengaging moments; for films, similarly ask trial viewers to mark stops on script copies if an automated analyzer is unavailable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budgeting and resource planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Slide shows can cost little more than labor, film, and processing, or be quite expensive with sophisticated equipment and specialized personnel. Look at how often your PR department will present slide shows before investing in expensive equipment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider renting equipment or contracting outside specialists if usage is infrequent. Use Gantt charts and network analyses for scheduling and cost/time tradeoffs; weigh in-house versus outside production for films.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan content before form (outline then visuals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Outline the major points of the presentation, still not worrying about the exact visuals. The content of the message should be decided before selecting the form; starting with visual images risks failing to set objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create an outline of main points first; then break outline into individual pieces of information and the visual images that will illustrate those concepts (split script).

rubrics_metrics.name: Split-script technique (concepts vs visuals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the concept (single piece of information) on one side of the planning sheet and the visual images on the other side; eventually come up with suggested shot(s) for each major and minor point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the split script to ensure each concept has an appropriate visual; helps coordinate separate teams preparing script and transparencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narration choices and coordination
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether narration will be live (more personal) or recorded (ensures accuracy and coordination); decide narrator type—authoritarian figure, professional-sounding announcer, or a realistic protagonist such as an employee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match narration style to objectives and audience; ensure narration length and content align with visuals (recorded narration helps precise synchronization).

rubrics_metrics.name: Match visuals to narration (avoid 'stalling')
rubrics_metrics.description: When the script has been written, it may be apparent if more shots are needed to fill sections; condensation of visuals may be necessary to prevent 'stalling' where insufficient narration covers the slides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure there is adequate narration for each slide cluster; add shots or condense visuals so visuals and script pace are aligned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Planning board / storyboard use
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare a planning board (storyboard) using index cards to sketch each shot and note what point the visual makes; arranging cards helps detect omission or repetition and achieve team consensus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use storyboards to visualize sequence, get manager approval, and include titles/credits/graphics so the art department can prepare them properly for filming or shooting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical faults: appropriate duration
rubrics_metrics.description: Show is Too Short: a selection of only a dozen slides held for two or three minutes may be boring unless each slide has great detail. Show Is Too Long: ordinarily, a slide show of ten to twenty minutes, followed by Q&A, is more enjoyable; hour-long presentations succeed only with a great amount of information or lively commentary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for roughly 10–20 minutes for a typical presentation; avoid padding to meet arbitrary scheduling constraints and tailor length to content and audience attention span.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical faults: pacing (too slow/too fast)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pace Is Too Slow or Too Fast: audiences dislike slides that flash too rapidly (important details missed) or an unvarying relentless pace (e.g., precisely 15 seconds per shot).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary pace by alternating slides that demand longer attention spans with rapid groups; for self-activated continuous shows the dynamic differs because the audience is not captive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical faults: redundancy and repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Slide Selection Is Redundant: many slightly different views (e.g., a dozen near-identical building shots) do not convey the message as well as two or three technically excellent shots. Major Points Are Inadequately Illustrated: each major point should be illustrated by a cluster of related visual information; audiences feel cheated by repeated use of the same images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose fewer, stronger images; ensure each major point has adequate, varied visual support; repetition of key slides may help but overuse is detrimental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Titles, charts, and graphics should organize and reinforce
rubrics_metrics.description: Title slides and other graphics such as tables and charts add professionalism, divide longer shows into manageable sections, provide transitions, and help reinforce major points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan titles and graphics from the beginning (one index card per title, color coded). Use titles to divide subject areas and reinforce transitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of titles/graphics (camera/lighting/design)
rubrics_metrics.description: All titles and graphics should be shot at the same time, with the same camera and lighting to assure consistency of color, brightness, and tone. Background colors, typefaces, and design elements should be harmonious with the photo transparencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain consistent visual design (colors linked to subject/product); if using computer-generated graphics, prepare/purchase them within budget for a cohesive look.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legibility and simplicity of titles/charts
rubrics_metrics.description: Hard-to-read titles and charts defeat their purpose: cluttering the slide with too much information, insufficient borders for visual relief, and type that is too small to be read from a few feet are common causes of illegibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep wording simple, leave borders, choose proper type height relative to viewing distance, ensure sufficient contrast, avoid overly fancy typefaces, and reuse repeated elements on movable pieces to save effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience tailoring and tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Never forget the makeup of the proposed audience (example: a jaunty stick-figure worked for middle-aged advertising salespersons but was 'corny' to college students). A slick look can give off a 'holier-than-thou' image detrimental to a campaign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt visuals, tone, and design to audience demographics and sensibilities; remove or alter elements that might provoke unintended reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use simple production methods when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep preparation simple: even PR people without art training can prepare title cards using transfer letters and nonreflective card stock; reuse repeated elements to save time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance production quality with available skills and budget — use affordable methods that achieve legibility and appropriate professionalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equipment selection and accessories
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose camera (35-mm reflex recommended), close-up and wide-angle lenses, tripod, cable release, copying stand, photoflood lights/reflectors for titling, an editing/viewing stand, proper storage (metal cabinets, compartmented plastic pages), and projectors with desired features (remote control, fade-dissolve, sound/visual synchronization).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base equipment purchasing on expected frequency of shows and required features; consider remote control, dissolve mechanisms, and synchronization add-ons; plan for lamp replacement and storage protection from heat/dust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projector/multimedia technique choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Slide projection is enhanced by multimedia approaches: dual-projector fade-dissolve (Kodak Carousel Dissolve Control), slide-tape synchronization (use silent cue on second track with a synchronizer), mosaic presentations (multi-projector wide-screen), or computer-coordinated preprogramming of projector and sound cues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select multimedia technique based on budget, desired effect, technical staff skill, and whether distribution to users without specialized equipment is required (synchronized versions may be infeasible for broad distribution).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper storage and handling of transparencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Heat, dust, and temperature extremes are the enemies of the transparency. Slides should be stored in their projection trays in a metal cabinet; out-takes and duplicates can be stored in compartmented clear plastic pages indexed in a heavy duty three-ring binder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep slides organized and protected to preserve image quality and ease of show assembly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Films must meet objectives and be evaluated
rubrics_metrics.description: As with photos and slide shows, films can maximize message retention and acceptance and help change attitudes and behaviors. Evaluate a film on a trial audience using questionnaires to measure communication effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Audience Analyzer equipment if available, or script-copy stop-recording as substitute; measure standard responses (interest, boredom, agreement, confusion) and correlate with film sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Film planning: synopsis, treatment, script, storyboard
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin with a synopsis (100-word summary), prepare a treatment (scene-by-scene explanation), then a script with camera directions and times. Prepare a storyboard showing each shot sketch, movement, camera actions, titles, credits, stills, and graphics so nontechnical managers can approve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the storyboard to get managerial approval and for detailed production planning; include instructions for special tints/effects so lab work fits the whole film.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select film format appropriate to distribution and quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Super-8 is cheap and easy and acceptable for documentation and displays (best with live narration), but most PR sound films use 16-mm for bright, clear images and better sound; 16-mm offers superior lab support for effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose Super-8 for low-cost, local use or spliced displays; choose 16-mm for distribution, television use, large auditoria, and when sound/effects support is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time scheduling and network analysis for film production
rubrics_metrics.description: Films take time and money; if a film must be done by a certain time, plan the sequence of production activities and use network analysis to avoid wasted time (e.g., crew waiting for a late scriptwriter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan production milestones, consider lead times for labs and edits, and decide on in-house vs outside producer early to budget appropriately.
